thread.title: Proposed legislation would lock North Carolina into expensive, outdated energy sources in a time of high bills and growing electricity demand
thread.title_full: Proposed legislation would lock North Carolina into expensive, outdated energy sources in a time of high bills and growing electricity demand

author: First State Times
title: Proposed legislation would lock North Carolina into expensive, outdated energy sources in a time of high bills and growing electricity demand
text:
Legislation introduced in the North Carolina House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 20 would require Duke Energy to continue operating its coal-fired power plants, which are among the most expensive sources of energy in the state. The proposed committee substitute for Senate Bill 730 also limits the economic selection of new, affordable sources of power.
The issue is significant as many North Carolina households face record-high electricity bills. The proposal could prevent families and businesses from accessing cheaper energy options like solar, wind, and battery storage. “At a time when North Carolina households are continuing to struggle with record-high electricity bills, this proposal puts much needed relief further out of reach by forcing families and businesses to rely on outdated, expensive, polluting coal plants,” said Will Scott, North Carolina Policy Director for Environmental Defense Fund. “Limiting North Carolina’s access to the lowest cost and fastest-to-build sources of power — solar, wind and battery storage – guarantees higher bills and more health-harming pollution for communities. North Carolina made a commitment to pursue affordable and reliable power — this proposal takes us in the wrong direction.”
A recent analysis commissioned by Environmental Defense Fund found that competitively procured clean energy has been over 40% cheaper than natural gas-powered electricity and 30% cheaper than coal over the last four years based on Duke Energy’s filings with the NC Utilities Commission. The same analysis shows that costs tied to Duke’s natural gas investments have contributed up to 67% of recent customer bill increases.
Last year lawmakers adopted S266—known as the “Power Bill Reduction Act”—despite independent findings that it would increase costs for residents. Since then, many customers have seen higher utility bills while Duke Energy has requested an additional rate hike for residential customers.
Senate Bill 730 also addresses concerns about rising data center development across North Carolina by proposing more local review for these projects. While it suggests some measures aimed at protecting customers from increased costs related to data center-driven upgrades in energy infrastructure, it does not allow developers to self-finance clean energy solutions that could keep those expenses off household electric bills.
“If affordability is truly the goal, this bill should allow data centers to pay for their own new, clean energy as other states are doing. Mandating continued coal power to meet growing data center demand is the worst of both worlds — higher costs and more pollution,” said Scott.
